definition.text: The expected value of an uncertain quantity is the average of its possible values, each weighted by how likely it is.

facts.text: It can be read as the long-run average result of repeating the same random experiment many times, as the law of large numbers shows.
For a fair six-sided die, whose faces 1 to 6 each have probability 1/6, the expected value is 3.5.
When all outcomes are equally likely, the expected value is simply the ordinary average.
It is usually written E(X), E[X] or EX; the letter E goes back to W. A. Whitworth in 1901.
The idea arose in the mid-17th century from the problem of points: how to split stakes fairly when a game ends early.
Pascal and Fermat solved it on the principle that a future gain is worth an amount proportional to the chance of getting it.
Christiaan Huygens published the first treatise on it in 1657, often seen as the first foundation of probability theory.
In decision theory, a person choosing under incomplete information is often assumed to maximise the expected value of their utility.

definition.text: An interest rate is the interest charged or paid each period, expressed as a share of the amount lent, deposited or borrowed.

facts.text: Rates are normally quoted per year.
Total interest depends on the rate together with the principal, how often interest compounds and the length of time.
Interest rates reflect a borrower's willingness to pay for money now rather than money in the future.
Firms borrow from banks expecting the borrowed capital to earn a return greater than the interest rate.
Riskier investments such as shares and junk bonds normally have to promise higher returns than safer government bonds.
Changing interest rates raises or lowers the opportunity cost of investing for firms.
The spread is the lending rate minus the deposit rate, and it covers banks' operating costs.

definition.text: The real interest rate is the interest rate after allowing for inflation, while the nominal rate is the rate before that adjustment.

facts.text: Real rates measure what is repaid against the buying power the money had when it was lent or invested.
If inflation equals the nominal rate, the real rate is zero.
The Fisher equation links real rates, nominal rates and the inflation rate; it can be used with projected (ex ante) or historical (ex post) rates.
Lenders and borrowers accept a nominal rate made up of the real rate they require plus the inflation they expect.
Real rates can be negative when nominal rates are below inflation.

definition.text: Central banks set target interest rates as a main tool for influencing investment, inflation and unemployment.

facts.text: Central banks usually cut rates when they want more investment and consumption in the economy.
Very low rates can be risky, feeding economic bubbles in property and stock markets.
The US federal funds rate varied between about 0.25% and 19% from 1954 to 2008.
A zero interest-rate policy sets the target near zero, where conventional monetary policy struggles because market rates are hard to push below zero.

title: Negative interest rate

definition.text: A negative interest rate charges savers for holding money and has been described as a tax on holding money.

facts.text: In theory lenders will not lend below 0% when they could hold cash instead, since that guarantees a loss.
Silvio Gesell proposed negative rates in the late 19th century.
The European Central Bank from 2014 and the Bank of Japan from early 2016 used negative rates alongside quantitative easing.
During the European debt crisis some countries' government bonds sold at negative yields.

definition.text: Liquidity preference is the tendency of people and firms to prefer holding cash or easily sold assets over harder-to-convert investments.

facts.text: It shows up as a yield gap between assets of different maturities and conversion costs.
It explains why longer-lasting assets usually have to offer higher yields.
